title: AQA GCSE English Literature Revision: Paper 1, Paper 2 & Exam Strategy
description: AQA GCSE English Literature revision guide covering Papers 1 and 2, closed-book study, essay structure, quotations, context, anthology and unseen poetry.

children: AQA GCSE English Literature is a closed-book qualification, so revision has to do two jobs at once: build secure knowledge of the texts and develop the analytical writing needed to use that knowledge under exam conditions.
How the AQA Literature exam is organised

Paper 1 covers Shakespeare and the 19th-century novel. It lasts 1 hour 45 minutes, carries 64 marks and is worth 40% of the GCSE. Paper 2 covers the modern text, anthology poetry and unseen poetry. It lasts 2 hours 15 minutes, carries 96 marks and is worth 60%.
Paper 1: Shakespeare using a printed extract and the play as a whole.
Paper 1: a 19th-century novel using a printed extract and the novel as a whole.
Paper 2: one modern prose or drama essay.
Paper 2: compare one named anthology poem with another poem from the same cluster.
Paper 2: analyse one unseen poem and then compare it with a second unseen poem.
Know the text as a network, not a plot

Plot knowledge is necessary but insufficient. Strong revision connects characters, themes, turning points and methods so that the same evidence can be adapted to different questions. A small set of versatile, well-understood references is more useful than a huge quotation list learned without interpretation.
Practise the move from evidence to argument

Students often know a quotation but do not know what to do with it. Practise a repeatable sequence: make a claim that answers the question, select precise evidence, analyse the writer's method, develop an interpretation, then connect that interpretation to the text as a whole.
Use context to illuminate the text
Context should sharpen interpretation rather than become a detached history paragraph. Ask how a relevant social, political or literary idea helps explain a writer's choice or an audience response.
Build a closed-book quotation system

Create compact quotation banks organised by theme and character. Each quotation should have more than one possible use. Retrieval practice is stronger when the quotation is recalled and then used in a sentence or paragraph rather than simply reread.

A useful weekly Literature routine
Retrieve quotations, characters and key moments.
Closely analyse one short extract or poem.
Plan a thesis and three analytical or comparative points.
Write one timed paragraph or essay section.
Review feedback and identify one specific next target.
